chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
title: George Jones and the Maestri patrons
summary: Dawson played trios in the big houses for patrons like Maestri, and describes George Jones, a rhyming singer with a sash-cord bass who made money from improvised songs.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: You can't tell what's going on in them places, you know, with the windows and the clothes up there. The whole man they had some stuff used to tell. Big like Lula White's old houses. I played music with, I used to play sometime with George Jones, you ever heard of him?

And we had trios. Well, uh, one of these big shots, you know, like Maester, you know, that Maester, Paul Maester, he was, uh, they had a clothing store on, uh, well, he had, he'd get around with them women and get a bunch of women and he'd go around from one place to the other, you know, buying champagne and stuff.

He'd want a band, he'd pick us up and, come on, let's go. And you did? We'd go in by a little white. Y'all want to go by? Yeah, yeah, sure. He'd know, we'd know what we was going to make, you see. And, uh, this fellow King, he was a big multi-milli- he was a big millionaire. Uh-huh. Uh, we wouldn't lose nothing. We'd make good money and drink us up in the house, you know, drink champagne with them women and all of them, having a good time. Mm-hmm. Until we get, until he get tired out and pay us off, you see.
Well, would George Jones get high? Would he climb up, uh, the high?
Oh, he, he had, he was supposed to be a bass player, but he had a bass, and didn't have no strings, he'd get the sash cord, you know, roll a sash. Ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha.
Do you remember his song about climbing up the, uh. We'd get having the strings. He'd take and make him a set of strings, you know.
And he sang all these dirty songs. The, the sash cord. And all of them be the same size, you know. Yeah. How could he play it then?

He did. He played. Man, he's tuned it up until he's getting high, you know. He'd, as long as it could make a bump. Boom, boom, boom. He'd be slapping, you know. He could rhyme, though. He made his money off of singing and rhyming. Yeah. I see, like he knew your name Clyde. Clyde, somebody tell you. Kind of, he found out he could, he could rhyme up a song on you, and you wouldn't, you think you was one and you'd be one and how he knew you, you see. He'd make up a rhyme on him. Doesn't know it's quite natural. You'd go around your pocket, give him a couple of dollars a piece. That's how he made his money.
Did you ever hit, you played guitar with him then? Yeah.

Madeline, most I played with Madeline Lee, you see. He'd have a guitar, I had Walter, uh, Walter of, uh, let's see, what Walter's name was. Been so long now. I know Walter, his name was Walter, guitar player. And he could sing too, you see. Him and Walter would sing and, uh, but he'd do all the rhyming. And I'd, I'd just play a lead part, anything he wanted to sing, I could play the lead part, you see, on a mandolin. Uh, he made, he was a hustler and he made, you go with him like a knight, when he get through the knockin' off, when he get ready to knock off, he was good for twenty-five or thirty dollars a piece. Easy.
